title: Meta Will Build a 168-Megawatt AI Data Centre Inside Ambani's Jamnagar Complex. Here Is Why It Matters.
excerpt: The deal deepens Meta's partnership with Reliance, positions India as an AI infrastructure hub, and arrives just as Anthropic's access restrictions have reignited the sovereign AI debate.
body:
Meta Platforms will lease an AI-ready data centre to be built by Mukesh Ambani's Reliance Industries in Jamnagar, Gujarat — a deal that deepens the American tech giant's ties with the Indian conglomerate and positions India as a serious contender in the global race for AI infrastructure.

The 168-megawatt facility, powered by energy equivalent to roughly 150,000 homes, will sit inside Reliance's flagship energy complex in western India. The project could be scaled up further, according to both companies, though neither disclosed financial terms or a completion date.

## Why Jamnagar

The site is not accidental. Jamnagar houses the world's largest oil refinery complex, but Reliance has been aggressively pivoting that infrastructure toward renewables and digital services. The data centre will draw power from Reliance's renewable energy assets on-site, reducing dependence on costlier grid electricity — a critical advantage in a country where power costs remain a barrier to hyperscale computing.

"Reliance has the infrastructure and Meta has the AI expertise," said Deven Choksey, managing director at DRChoksey FinServ in Mumbai. "Jamnagar offers a strategic edge with ready access to power, water and infrastructure at lower cost."

## The Bigger Play

Meta is already one of the largest investors in Reliance's IPO-bound Jio Platforms, having bought a $5.7 billion stake in 2020. Last year, the two companies formed a joint venture to develop enterprise AI tools using Meta's Llama models. The data centre deal extends that partnership from software into physical infrastructure — the kind of long-term bet that signals Meta sees India not just as a market for its consumer apps, but as a base for training and running AI workloads.

The deal comes amid a surge of hyperscale data centre investment in India. Amazon, Microsoft, and Google have all announced major expansions. In February, Reliance committed approximately $110 billion in new investments across AI, telecom, and energy, while the Adani Group outlined $100 billion of its own. The Indian government has offered foreign companies a more than 20-year tax break for using local data centres, sweetening the economics considerably.

India's data centre market is projected to nearly double to $13.11 billion by 2034, according to consulting firm IMARC Group, driven by digitalisation, cloud adoption, and rising AI workloads.

## Sovereign AI at a Crossroads

The timing is significant. Just days ago, Anthropic suspended access to its newest AI models in India, reigniting a debate about whether the country can afford to remain dependent on a handful of foreign frontier AI providers. Tech leaders including Mohandas Pai and Zoho's Srinivasan Vembu have demanded a $6 billion sovereign AI fund. TCS partnered with Anthropic to equip 50,000 employees with Claude — but the partnership was announced the same week that Anthropic pulled access, underscoring the fragility of relying on external providers.

Meta's Llama models, by contrast, are open-source — a distinction that gives the Reliance-Meta partnership a different flavour. Indian startups and enterprises can build on Llama without the risk of a foreign company unilaterally restricting access. That philosophical difference may prove more important than the data centre's raw capacity.

## What the Diaspora Should Know

For NRIs in tech, the Meta-Reliance deal is a signal that India's AI infrastructure story is accelerating beyond government promises and into concrete, funded projects. The data centre will create high-skilled jobs in Gujarat, generate demand for Indian AI talent, and potentially serve as a regional hub for Meta's AI operations across South Asia and the Middle East.

For Indian investors, Jio Platforms' IPO — widely expected to be one of the largest in history — now has another marquee anchor in its partnership portfolio. And for the broader diaspora watching India's economic trajectory, the deal is a reminder that the country's tech ambitions are no longer speculative. They are being poured in concrete, wired with fibre, and plugged into 168 megawatts of power in a refinery town in western Gujarat.
